page: Amazon Web Services m8a.metal-24xl is a bare-metal general-purpose server driven by a 96-core AMD EPYC 9R45 processor built on the x86_64 architecture. Offering 96 dedicated physical cores running at up to 4.5 GHz with a single thread per core, the bare-metal architecture circumvents hypervisor virtualization overhead. The configuration integrates 384.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory operating at 6 GHz, supplying a balanced 4.0 GB per core. The processor incorporates vector processing flags including AVX-512 with VNNI and BF16 support, along with hardware-level AMD SVM virtualization extensions.

The server does not include onboard local storage, requiring network-attached storage architectures for all persistent data requirements. Network performance is anchored by a 40 Gbps baseline throughput profile, and the instance allocates zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses. Lacking discrete graphics processing units, data processing relies on the 96 AMD CPU cores and the DDR5 subsystem, which demonstrates memory bandwidth reaching 521.53 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads and 228.28 GB/sec for uncached writes.

Benchmark results place the m8a.metal-24xl in the top 10 percent of evaluated systems for multi-core compute capacity. The server achieves a Geekbench multi-core score of 30,617, a PassMark CPU score of 139,481.72, and strong results in Clang software compilation and cryptographic routines. High memory throughput is reflected in over 242 million Redis SET operations per second and 107.49 GB/sec in static web serving throughput. CPU-based inference workloads achieve 74.17 text generation tokens per second on 7B parameter language models. These characteristics align with demanding workloads such as multi-threaded continuous integration pipelines, high-throughput database clusters, and dense web tier services.

It contains no onboard local storage or discrete GPUs, relying on network-attached storage solutions. This hardware profile provides high compute density and memory bandwidth for heavy multi-threaded workloads, including high-throughput database clusters, large software compilation pipelines, static web serving fleets, and CPU-based machine learning inference.
